title: Call me bitter (Ruth 1:1–21)
hookLine: Naomi loses husband and sons in Moab and asks to be called Mara, bitter
carry: stay beside them, let their words stand
tomorrow: Thy people shall be my people (Ruth 1:16–17)
last: THEY PRAISE, THEY DOUBT, THEY COMPLAIN.

cards: Two women walk into Bethlehem, dusty from the road, and the whole town comes out to look. In the King James, "all the city was moved about them, and they said, Is this Naomi?" She left with a husband and two sons.

She's come back with none of them, and the woman beside her is a foreigner from Moab. The neighbors aren't cruel. They're just shocked; they can barely match the face they knew to the one in front of them.
And Naomi answers in a way nobody expects. She tells them to stop using her name.

teach.h: A FAMINE, MOAB, AND THREE GRAVES.
teach.b: Go back to how the book begins: "in the days when the judges ruled," a famine in the land. A man of Bethlehem, Elimelech, takes his wife Naomi and their two sons to the fields of Moab to survive. There Elimelech dies.
The sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. Then both sons die.
The King James puts it in one bare line: "the woman was left of her two sons and her husband." Left. That's the word for her.
When she hears there's bread again at home, she sets out, and on the road she begs her daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers. Orpah, weeping, goes. Ruth won't.
That moment is tomorrow's. Today belongs to Naomi at the city gate.

teach.h: CALL ME NOT NAOMI, CALL ME MARA.
teach.b: "Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me." Mara means bitter. Then: "I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty."
Notice three things. First, she says it out loud, in public, and she says it about God; she doesn't pretend to be fine for the neighbors. Second, the book doesn't correct her.
No one tells her to look on the bright side, and her words are kept, exactly as she said them, in Scripture.

teach.h: SHE SAYS EMPTY, AND RUTH IS THERE.
teach.b: Third, the quiet ache: when Naomi says empty, Ruth is standing right next to her, the one person who stayed. Grief that deep can't see it yet, and the story doesn't rush her.
It only adds that they arrived at the beginning of barley harvest.

how: The book of Ruth is read in synagogue on Shavuot, and Jews count it among the short scrolls of the Writings.

o: empty-handed: the word for a widow with no sons
bitter: the name Naomi asks to be called in her grief
a foreigner: what Bethlehem calls Ruth at the gate

games.q: call me bitter — tap the pairs.

s: the book scolds Naomi for complaining about God
it keeps her words exactly as she said them, and no one corrects her.
Naomi lost her husband and both her sons in Moab
"the woman was left of her two sons and her husband."
Naomi comes home to Bethlehem alone
Ruth is right beside her when she says empty.

games.q: you're Naomi at the gate of Bethlehem. the whole town asks, is this Naomi? what do you say?
o: call me not Naomi, call me Mara.
games.why: she asks for a new name: "call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me."

practice: Bring to mind one person carrying a heavy loss, a death, a divorce, a home, a job, a body that doesn't work the way it did.

Don't fix it or find the bright side for them; in your mind, just stand beside them at the gate, saying nothing, staying, the way the book lets Naomi be. If you pray, you can hold them before God without words.

wordCard.voice: Mara. Hebrew for bitter, the name Naomi asks to be called, and the book lets her say it. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: bitter, the name Naomi asks to be called in Ruth 1:20.

carryVoice: Your line: stay beside them, let their words stand. The book keeps Naomi's words. That's day eight hundred thirty-four.
